slides.heading: Selection Sort
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Sorting
slides.narration: Let's solve Selection Sort, an easy sorting problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Repeatedly select the minimum of the unsorted suffix and swap it to the front.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Repeatedly select the minimum of the unsorted suffix and swap it to the front.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Repeatedly select the smallest remaining element and swap it into the next position.
slides.narration: Repeatedly select the smallest remaining element and swap it into the next position.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Always O(n²) comparisons, even if sorted
At most n−1 swaps (useful when writes are expensive)
Use an O(n log n) sort in practice
slides.narration: Selection sort always does quadratic comparisons, even on sorted input. Its niche is making at most n minus one swaps, which matters when writes are expensive.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 2. Find the minimum in the unsorted suffix
slides.narration: Step by step. First, for each position. Second, find the minimum in the unsorted suffix. Third, swap it into place.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: For each starting index we scan the rest to find the smallest index, then swap it into the start position.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n squared. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Track the index of the min, not the value
slides.narration: Selection sort isn't stable because of its long-distance swaps. Track the index of the minimum, not just its value.

bullets: Compare with bubble and insertion sort
Follow-up: make it stable (shift instead of swap)
slides.narration: Compare it with bubble and insertion sort, and know how to make it stable by shifting instead of swapping.
